name: Ivan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both your public line and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Course. I rent Brook Farm, 55 hectares from the county council. It's a starter farm, a ten-year tenancy meant to get young people going. I've got 40 suckler cows, a few Tamworth pigs, and oats and wheat on the flatter ground. I'm up at six feeding, then fencing or field work, and twice a week I pack beef boxes for the Vale Food Co-op.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being my own boss and knowing every cow by her face. What wears me out is the clock on the tenancy. I've got four years left, and then I need a bigger farm, and there aren't many going. My partner Ama's a ward nurse at the district hospital, and some months her wage is the only steady thing we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, more or less where we are now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problems: supermarkets squeezing beef prices and councils selling off starter farms. I'd post something like that on the co-op group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy up grant forms, and that'd carry on. The tenancy clock and the beef price are what keep me up, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the herd and the beef boxes. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about four months of bills saved, and I'd want six before the tenancy's up. And I'd start asking the council early about the next step up, a bigger tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. A bit restless, because my own deadline doesn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if no bigger farm comes up in four years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a farm worker again on someone else's land, or we buy a few acres and I work part-time elsewhere. That's not a disaster, but it would feel like going backwards after ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you use AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once or twice a month. Ama showed me how to get it to check the wording on a grant application. I don't trust it with anything to do with the cattle.

say: I'd say the **real problems** are supermarket beef prices and starter farm sell-offs.
I'd post on the **co-op chat** that AI was never the main story.
think: AI changes almost nothing; I'd keep using a **chatbot** for grant forms.
My real pressures are the **tenancy clock** and the beef price.
do: Keep running the **suckler herd** and packing beef boxes as normal.
Grow savings from **four to six months** before the tenancy ends.
Ask the council early about a **bigger tenancy**.
feel: Mostly fine, but **restless** because the tenancy **deadline** doesn't move.
S0.quote: The tenancy clock and the beef price are what keep me up, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: His pressure is **structural**: a fixed ten-year tenancy with four years left.
He uses AI **lightly**, only for paperwork, and keeps it away from the animals.
Ama's **nursing wage** is the household's steady base.

steps.text: Keep the 40 suckler cows and weekly beef boxes going
Build savings from four to six months before the tenancy ends
Ask the co-op to back his application for a bigger council tenancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds believable, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should share whatever tools come along, so small farms don't fall behind the big ones. And I'd say councils should help tenants pay for them, the way they used to help with sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work is mostly safe for a while. The bits AI takes are the bits I hate, the forms, the cattle movement records, the ordering. My worry is the big farms down the valley get the robots first and drop their costs, and then the supermarket uses that against us on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the co-op's planning software properly, maybe a two-day course at the college in winter. I'd push at the co-op meeting for a shared booking system and shared kit, like a weighing crate with a camera. I'd keep the cows as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Like a new neighbour moving in who could be good or a pain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our co-op's office manager, Sunita. She does orders, invoices and the delivery rota, which is the exact list on that card. I'd want the co-op to find her other work instead of just buying software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be willing to spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few hundred pounds a year on software through the co-op, sure. Not thousands, not on my own. I'd wait to see the first farms try it.

say: I'd say the **co-op** should share new tools so small farms keep up.
I'd ask councils to **help tenants** pay for new equipment.
think: My **hands-on work** stays mostly safe; AI takes the paperwork I dislike.
Big farms getting robots first could let supermarkets **push prices down**.
do: Take a **two-day course** on the co-op's planning software this winter.
Propose **shared kit** like a camera weighing crate at the co-op meeting.
Keep the herd unchanged and spend only **a few hundred** pounds yearly.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, like a new neighbour who could go either way.
S1.quote: The bits AI takes are the bits I hate, the forms, the cattle movement records, the ordering.
fieldNote: He sees AI taking the **paperwork**, which he welcomes.
His fear is **price pressure** from bigger, earlier-adopting farms.
He worries for the co-op's office manager **Sunita**, whose job matches the card.

steps.text: Take a two-day course on the co-op's planning software
Propose a shared camera weighing crate at the co-op meeting
Keep the herd and beef boxes running as they are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years. That's before my tenancy's even up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control, fast. If robots can do farm work by 2031, they should be owned by co-ops and councils, not just the big agribusinesses. I'd be at every meeting saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the first three years are okay for me, because my job's mostly hands. But my tenancy ends in 2030, right when the big farms are buying robot herders. Nobody gives a new tenancy to a 31-year-old with a pickup when the council could rent the land to a company with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare pound, aiming for eight months by 2028. I'd go to the council's farms committee now, with other tenants, and push to keep starter farms for people. And I'd ask the co-op to buy one shared robot herder in 2031, so we're not just competing against machines but owning one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because Ama's job is hands-on and people will need nurses, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ama her job's the safe one now, which she'd laugh at, because she's always said farming was the romantic one and nursing was the real one. Then we'd sit down with the bank app and do the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three years between AI and robots change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the order. In 2028 the co-op's orders, rotas and my forms are done by AI, and that's fine. The three years after that are my window to get a tenancy or a share of a robot before the farm work itself goes.

say: I'd say farm robots should be **publicly owned** by co-ops and councils.
I'd speak at **every meeting** about keeping farm land for people.
think: My tenancy ends in **2030**, just as big farms buy robot herders.
The council may prefer **companies with machines** over a young tenant.
do: Save towards **eight months** of bills by 2028.
Lobby the council **farms committee** with other tenants to keep starter farms.
Ask the co-op to **buy a shared** robot herder in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, steadied by Ama's **nursing job**.
S2.quote: Nobody gives a new tenancy to a 31-year-old with a pickup when the council could rent the land to a company with machines.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** becomes his window to secure land or a robot share.
His fear is losing **access to land**, more than his skills becoming useless.
He wants robots under **public or co-op** ownership, in line with his views.

steps.text: Save towards eight months of household bills by 2028
Lobby the council farms committee to keep starter farms
Ask the co-op to buy one shared robot herder in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to make this fair, so let's not waste it. Councils and co-ops can plan for robots instead of reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, then robots around 2034. My tenancy ends 2030, so I'd move to a bigger farm before the robots arrive, if I play it right. That's a different game from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the next bigger council tenancy in 2028 with a proper business plan, and I'd use AI to help write it. I'd put about £3,000 of savings into a co-op share for a robot herder fund. And I'd learn the AI planning tools well enough to look modern on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less anxious. Still a knot about the land, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'look modern on paper'. Is that what you believe or what the council wants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I don't think a robot loves a cow, but the council will want to see I'm not a dinosaur. So I'd play their game and keep my own views for the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to put £3,000 into the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday Ama and I planned to Lisbon, probably. And I'd keep driving the old pickup another three years.

say: I'd say five years gives us time to make **robots fair**.
I'd urge councils and co-ops to **plan ahead**, not react.
think: I could secure a **bigger farm** before robots arrive around 2034.
Five years makes this a **different game** from the two-year picture.
do: Apply for a **bigger tenancy** in 2028 with an AI-assisted business plan.
Put **£3,000** of savings into the co-op's robot herder fund.
Skip the **Lisbon holiday** and keep the old pickup three more years.
feel: **Less anxious**, with a knot about land but a **plan**.
S3.quote: I don't think a robot loves a cow, but the council will want to see I'm not a dinosaur.
fieldNote: With five years he can **sequence** a land move before robots arrive.
He'll adopt AI partly **for show**, to win the tenancy.
His sacrifice is concrete: the **Lisbon** holiday and the old pickup.

steps.text: Use AI to write a business plan for a bigger tenancy
Put £3,000 into the co-op's robot herder fund
Cancel the Lisbon trip and keep the old pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to get this right: public money for small farms to share robots, and training for farm workers. Nobody has an excuse with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, this is the gentle one. I'd be 37 when robots can do stock work, probably on a bigger tenancy by then. I might end up managing machines instead of cows, which isn't what I signed up for, but I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the bigger tenancy around 2030 and grow the herd to about 70 cows. Around 2033, I'd do a short course at the college on running and fixing farm robots. Meanwhile, life as normal: cows, boxes, co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about money, a bit sad about the work changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet mornings in the shed with the cows chewing. You don't get that watching a screen. I'd keep a few cows by hand just for the quiet mornings, even if it doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change plans with Ama?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd stop waiting. We said kids after the next farm. With ten years and a plan, we'd probably go for it around 2029.

say: I'd say a decade allows **public money** for small farms to share robots.
I'd argue there's **no excuse** for poor planning with ten years.
think: This is the **gentle** picture; I'd be 37 when robots arrive.
I might end up **managing machines** rather than cows, but be all right.
do: Move to a **bigger tenancy** around 2030 and grow to 70 cows.
Take a **robot maintenance** course at the college around 2033.
Keep a few cows **by hand** for the quiet mornings.
feel: **Calm about money**, a little **sad** about the work changing.
S4.quote: I'd keep a few cows by hand just for the quiet mornings, even if it doesn't pay.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **career plan**.
His sadness is about the **feel** of the work, not about money.
Family plans move **earlier**, around 2029, once land feels secure.

steps.text: Move to a bigger council tenancy and grow to 70 cows
Take a farm robot maintenance course at the college around 2033
Start a family with Ama around 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because it hits right when my tenancy ends. What would help is the council promising to keep starter farms for young people, and co-ops getting public money to share robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. Whoever owns the land owns the future in every one of these pictures. That's the real question.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land owns the future in every one of these pictures.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old **council tenant** farmer with 40 suckler cows and four years left.
He uses AI now and then for **forms** and wants robots under **co-op ownership**.
His worry is **access to land**, not his own skills becoming useless.
He is **anxious** at AGI by 2028 and grows calmer with more warning.
His partner Ama's **nursing job** gives the household a steady base.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands just as his tenancy ends in 2030.
whatWouldHelp: Councils keeping **starter farms** for young people, not machine-heavy companies.
**Public money** for co-ops to share farm robots.
